title: Conjugates, magnitude, division, and equations
objective: Use conjugation and magnitude identities, divide by nonzero complex numbers including axis cases, and solve and verify a linear complex equation.
why: Conjugation connects complex arithmetic to distance. It turns a complex denominator into a positive real number, makes reciprocals understandable, and gives a direct way to verify a solution.

sections.heading: Quick recall
paragraphs: For z=a+bi, its conjugate is a-bi. Its magnitude is |z|=√(a²+b²), the distance from the origin. Multiplying a number by its conjugate gives its squared magnitude: $z\overline z=a^2+b^2$.
To divide by w≠0, multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of w. The resulting real denominator is |w|². Check the quotient by multiplying it by the original divisor.

sections.heading: A reflection is not an additive inverse
paragraphs: Conjugation keeps the real coordinate and reverses the imaginary coordinate. It reflects a point across the real axis. Negating a complex number reverses both coordinates, which rotates its direction halfway around the origin.

Conjugating twice returns the starting point. A number equals its own conjugate exactly when its imaginary coefficient is zero, so every real number is unchanged. Conjugation also respects sums and products; you can conjugate the result or conjugate each operand first.

sections.heading: Magnitude measures distance
paragraphs: The real and imaginary axes meet at right angles, so the Pythagorean theorem gives |a+bi|=√(a²+b²). Magnitude is a real, nonnegative value. It equals zero only at the complex zero; it never becomes negative because an individual coordinate is negative.

In $(a+bi)(a-bi)$ the cross terms cancel. The remaining term -b²i² becomes +b², giving a²+b². This is the squared magnitude, not the magnitude itself. Taking the nonnegative square root recovers the distance.

sections.heading: Why the conjugate creates a reciprocal
paragraphs: For nonzero w, the identity w·conjugate(w)=|w|² lets us divide both sides by the positive real number |w|². Thus $w^{-1}=\overline w/|w|^2$. Multiplying w by this expression gives 1, which is precisely the defining property of a reciprocal.

Complex division z/w means z times that reciprocal. Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same nonzero conjugate preserves the quotient, just as multiplying a real fraction by a/a preserves its value. Keep parentheses around both numerator factors while distributing.

sections.heading: Axis cases and the forbidden zero
paragraphs: A purely real divisor is valid unless it is zero. A purely imaginary divisor is also valid unless it is zero: for example, 1/i=-i because i(-i)=1. The condition c²+d²>0 checks both cases at once.

Division by zero is undefined. If z≠0, no value q can satisfy 0q=z. If z=0, every q satisfies 0q=0, so that equation cannot specify a unique quotient either. Neither case gives a defined value for z/0.

sections.heading: Solve an equation and check the original statement
paragraphs: In αz=β with α≠0, multiply both sides by α⁻¹ to get z=β/α. This step produces a candidate, but substituting it into the original equation provides an independent arithmetic check. A product-back check is especially useful when a conjugate or subtraction sign may have been lost.

If α=0, inspect β instead of dividing. The equation 0z=0 permits every complex number, while 0z=β with β≠0 has no solution. The independent exercises here focus on a unique solution with a nonzero coefficient.

examples.title: Reflect one coordinate
examples.prompt: Compare the conjugate and negative of z=-2+5i.

steps.reason: Conjugation reverses only the imaginary coefficient.
The additive inverse reverses both coordinates.

examples.conclusion: These two operations agree only when the real part is zero.

examples.title: Distance and its square

steps.reason: Distance uses squared coordinates and the nonnegative square root.
The conjugate product equals the squared distance.

examples.conclusion: The magnitude is 5; the squared magnitude is 25.

examples.title: Conjugate twice
examples.prompt: Conjugate 3-2i twice and explain what happens to a real number.

steps.reason: Two sign reversals restore the imaginary coefficient.
A real number has no imaginary displacement to reflect.

examples.conclusion: Every real number is its own conjugate.

examples.title: Build a reciprocal

steps.reason: Multiply top and bottom by the denominator's conjugate.
The positive real denominator is the squared magnitude.

examples.conclusion: The reciprocal is not obtained by separately inverting the components.

steps.reason: The numerator is 3+5i+2i²=1+5i; the denominator is 2.
Multiplying the quotient back recovers the numerator.

examples.title: Divisors on either axis

steps.reason: A nonzero imaginary divisor has a valid positive squared magnitude.
A real scalar divides both coordinates.

examples.conclusion: Neither nonzero axis case is excluded from complex division.

examples.title: Reject a zero divisor
examples.prompt: Can either 3/0 or 0/0 define one complex value?

steps.reason: Multiplication by zero cannot recover a nonzero numerator.
This does not select a unique quotient.
The coefficient is nonzero, so division is permitted.
Substitution verifies the result in the original equation.

guided.title: Finish the reasoning
guided.setup: Divide 4+2i by 1+i, then verify the quotient.
before: The denominator becomes 2 and the numerator becomes 6-2i.

question.prompt: Give the exact quotient and the result of multiplying it by the original denominator.
hints: Identify the nonzero divisor and its conjugate first.
The denominator becomes 2 and the numerator becomes 6-2i.
explanation: The check (3-i)(1+i)=4+2i recovers the original numerator.
question.answerSummary: (6-2i)/2=3-i. The check (3-i)(1+i)=4+2i recovers the original numerator.

guided.after: Explain the reasoning before starting independent practice. Guided feedback is assisted work, not checkpoint evidence.

interaction.prompt: Change a numerator and denominator. Predict the denominator's conjugate, squared magnitude, and quotient. Reveal reflected points, the quotient, and a product-back check. Set the denominator to zero and inspect the explicit undefined-state message.

summary: Conjugation reflects the imaginary coordinate; negation reverses both coordinates.
Magnitude is nonnegative and its square equals the conjugate product.
Only zero is forbidden as a complex divisor.
Verify division and linear equations by multiplying back.
retrieval: Without notes, find the conjugate and magnitude of 1-2i, then use them to find its reciprocal. Explain why dividing by 2i is valid but dividing by zero is not.
